clue.text: Primarily servile role taken by Bill, American slave

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so only the opening letter of servile is used

parts.note: an actor's role is a part
a bill is an account, abbreviated AC

explanation.surface: A servile part in a play is written by someone called Bill, playing an American slave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken by' just joins the pieces; Bill is an account (AC), not a name.
explanation.definitionFit: Spartacus was the Thracian gladiator who led the great slave revolt against Rome.

clue.text: Society type in fine material

parts.note: ilk means type or kind, as in 'people of that ilk'

explanation.surface: A fashionable society type is dressed in fine fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Silk is a luxurious fabric spun by silkworms, the classic example of fine cloth.

clue.text: A superior god seen as creator

parts.note: U stands for upper-class, so superior in the social sense
Thor is the Norse god of thunder

explanation.surface: A lofty deity is regarded as the maker of all things.
explanation.walkthrough: U for upper-class is a long-standing British label for 'posh' usage.
explanation.definitionFit: A writer is the originator of a work, so the word is a synonym for creator.

clue.text: Male piggies eating ace food items

indicators.note: eating means taking something inside, so the ace goes within the male piggies

parts.note: a tom is a male cat
piggies is nursery talk for toes, as in 'this little piggy'
A is the card abbreviation for ace

explanation.surface: Boar pigs are munching on a first-rate meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'piggies' suggests pigs, but it is the toes of the nursery rhyme.
explanation.definitionFit: Tomatoes are fruits eaten as vegetables, so they count as items of food.

clue.text: Specially-made domestic screws, useless for insertion

indicators.note: for insertion says this piece is to be placed inside the jumbled letters
screws means twists out of shape, so the letters of domestic are rearranged

parts.note: US is an informal abbreviation for useless, from 'unserviceable'

explanation.surface: Household screws made to order turn out to be useless for fitting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'screws' looks like hardware but is the anagram signal, making CUSTOMIED; 'for insertion' puts the useless abbreviation inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something altered to suit a particular buyer is tailor-made, i.e. built to order.

clue.text: It may help to get sporting event off with a bang

definitions.text: It may help to get sporting event off with a bang

parts.words: It may help to get sporting event off with a bang
parts.note: a race begins when an official fires a blank shot, literally starting it with a bang

explanation.surface: A sporting event begins with a bang.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off with a bang' sounds like the figurative great start, but here the bang is real.
explanation.definitionFit: The gun fired to begin a race is what makes the runners set off, with a literal bang.

clue.text: See servant dash up to provide a bit of business information

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the letters are read from the bottom, i.e. backwards

parts.note: a page is a boy servant
to dash is to dart, rush quickly

explanation.surface: A servant rushes upstairs to deliver some business news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' is only a link here, inviting the solver to look at what follows.
explanation.definitionFit: The difference between a country's imports and exports is an economic statistic, a piece of business data.

clue.text: Scientist's introduction to rare work included by one making literary selection

indicators.note: included by says these letters go inside the following piece

parts.note: someone who compiles a selection of poems or stories is an anthologist

indicators.note: an introduction is the start, so only the first letter of rare is used

parts.note: OP is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: A scientist writes the introduction to a rare work in someone's literary collection.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after Scientist is a link meaning 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a scientist who studies human societies and cultures.

clue.text: Complaint from a visitor, not good person

indicators.note: not says the good person is left out of the visitor

parts.note: a guest is a visitor
ST is short for saint, a good person

explanation.surface: A grumble comes from a house guest who is not a nice person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' reads as a grumble but means an illness.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an old word for a malarial fever, and complaint can mean an ailment or illness.

clue.text: Bit of hair in phone — hindrance

parts.note: to phone someone is to ring them
let is an old word for hindrance, as in 'without let or hindrance', and a tennis term

explanation.surface: A strand of hair gets in the way of the phone.
explanation.definitionFit: A curl or lock is a small piece of hair.

clue.text: Horse 'as to be executed

parts.note: has to means must; the apostrophe shows a dropped H, as in Cockney speech
be executed means hang, and with the dropped H of the same speech it becomes 'ang

explanation.surface: A Cockney declares that the horse has got to be put to death.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe on 'as signals H-dropping speech, which also applies to hang.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a wild or half-wild horse of the American plains.

clue.text: Author had set about novel finally

indicators.note: set about suggests something knocked around, so the letters of had are rearranged
finally picks the last letter of novel

explanation.surface: A writer had begun tackling a novel at last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set about' looks like 'started on', but signals the anagram of HAD giving DAH.
explanation.definitionFit: Roald Dahl was a British writer of children's books such as Matilda.

clue.text: Men in action in Old Trafford pharmacy?

definitions.meaning: troops deployed in a combat zone rather than air power
a Boots chemist sitting on the football ..., Boots being a British high-street pharmacy chain

explanation.surface: Players in a match at Manchester United's stadium need a chemist.
explanation.walkthrough: Old Trafford is Manchester United's football ground; Boots is the best-known British chain of chemists.
explanation.definitionFit: The military phrase refers to soldiers physically deployed in a conflict zone.

clue.text: A son eating badly generates anger

definitions.note: the clue gives a third-person verb phrase where the answer is the base form of the verb

indicators.note: badly says the letters are put together wrongly, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A son who eats with poor manners makes people cross.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly' looks as if it describes the eating, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To provoke hostility in someone is to make them cross, so the verb means stir up anger.

clue.text: See 12
Territorial lion bursting with rage

indicators.note: bursting means breaking apart, so the letters of lion and rage are scattered and reassembled

explanation.surface: A lion defending its patch explodes with fury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' is a link joining the two parts of the anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words relate to a particular area or district, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Winding trail to lake in sandy area?

indicators.note: a winding path twists about, so the letters of trail to are rearranged

parts.note: L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A twisting path leads down to a lake through dunes.
explanation.definitionFit: The shore zone between high and low tide is often sand, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Member of tribe maybe sweeps English off isle

indicators.note: off says the English is removed from the sweeping word

parts.note: sweeping is one example of how someone cleans
the Isle of Man lies in the Irish Sea

explanation.surface: A tribesman perhaps clears the English off his island.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottish clan is a family-based tribe, so one of its men is a tribe member.

clue.text: Infant only briefly to be kept by poor labourer? It's likely

indicators.note: kept by means held inside, so the shortened infant sits within the labourer

parts.note: prole, short for proletarian, is a member of the working class

indicators.note: only briefly says the word is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: an infant is a baby

explanation.surface: A struggling worker is probably going to look after a baby for a short while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's' is a link before the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something expected to happen is probable, a direct synonym for likely.

clue.text: Remove blemish, as you might think, from nasty ruler?

parts.note: the prefix de- means remove, as in de-ice or de-bug
a spot is a blemish

explanation.surface: Clearing a spot off a cruel dictator, as you might imagine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as you might think' admits the answer looks as if it means 'remove spots'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tyrant is an oppressive absolute ruler, which fits nasty ruler.

clue.text: State measure that brings pain all around

indicators.note: all around says the pain encloses the measure

parts.note: a pang is a sharp pain
an en is a printer's measure of width

explanation.surface: Someone states a measure that only increases the pain all round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State' looks like a verb, but it is the definition: a state of Malaysia.
explanation.definitionFit: This is one of the constituent states of Malaysia, an island off the west coast.

clue.text: No amateur person starting an organisation could be more sincere

parts.note: a professional is no amateur
someone who establishes an organisation is its founder

explanation.surface: A professional who founds a company might be more earnest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' is a link before the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Deeper feeling is greater sincerity, so the comparative of 'deep' fits more sincere.

clue.text: Exclamation of relief not many heard

indicators.note: heard means we take the sound of the word rather than its spelling

parts.note: few means not many

explanation.surface: Only a handful of people heard a sigh of relief.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the interjection people utter when an anxiety passes.

clue.text: City that's old and in no hurry for the most part

indicators.note: for the most part means most of the word is kept, dropping its last letter

parts.note: someone in no hurry is slow

explanation.surface: An ancient city that is mostly unhurried.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the capital city of Norway.

clue.text: British embracing Irish somewhere in Offaly

indicators.note: embracing means hugging, so British wraps around Irish

explanation.surface: A Briton hugs an Irish person somewhere in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: Offaly is a county in the Irish midlands.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a market town in County Offaly in the middle of Ireland.

clue.text: Smile wryly about the thing that characterises some snobs?

definitions.text: Smile wryly about the thing that characterises some snobs?

indicators.note: about says the rearranged letters go round the next piece
wryly means in a twisted way, so the letters of smile are rearranged

parts.note: it is the pronoun for a thing

explanation.surface: Smirking knowingly about something is a snobbish trait.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wryly' shuffles SMILE into ELISM, which goes 'about' IT; the whole clue also describes snobbery.
explanation.definitionFit: Belief in the superiority of a select few is the attitude of snobs, shown in a superior smile.

clue.text: Unknown character performing in operatic song somewhere in America

indicators.note: in places these letters inside the operatic song

parts.note: an aria is a solo song in an opera
Z is an algebraic unknown, like x and y
someone performing is on, on stage

explanation.surface: A mystery figure sings a solo in an opera set somewhere in America.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a south-western US state, home of the Grand Canyon.

clue.text: Youngster went, eager to have a change of direction

indicators.note: a change of direction suggests the letters are turned about and rearranged

explanation.surface: A child set off, keen to try a different route.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' is a link joining fodder and anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A child between about ten and twelve, nearly a teenager, is a youngster.
